fetched_contents.text: Modeling wind turbine blades by geometrically-exact beam and shell elements: A comparative approach Introduction The total wind power capacity installed in the world increased approximately 17% in 2015, rising from 369 GW to 432 GW, as presented by the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC) [1]. Even with possibilities of novel conceptions for wind turbines, a very important and still most often used model is the horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT) [2]. Throughout its history, HAWT has significantly evolved from a power of 25 kW, with a rotor diameter of 10 m, to 6 MW with a rotor diameter of 164 m [3]. Recent studies for a 10 MW offshore HAWT [4] are being conducted. In this context, the main reason for the increasing size of wind turbines is that their power capacity is directly related to the area covered by the blades, and therefore, related to the square of their length. However, the increase of the length of blades is not a trivial engineering process. Assumptions and models previously used for short blades may be inappropriate for the new proposals. In fact, slender and flexible wind turbine blades may experience high nonlinear structural behavior. Furthermore, aeroelasticity may play a role. As a consequence, considerable research is being employed to produce realistic wind turbine blade models. There are basically three main approaches to establishing structural numerical models for analysis of wind turbine blades. When there is an interest in local structural issues, a 3D model composed of solid finite elements provides extreme details for stress distributions, in detriment of a very high computational cost. However, it usually cannot be used to model structural global behavior. For that, a 3D model based on shell finite elements may be proposed. It simplifies local details, but usually is also a good compromise to analyze overall structural behavior, still predicting important phenomena such as local buckling. A third approach, the computationally cheapest one, is based on 3D beam structural assumptions. It may be used as a very efficient approach for the initial design of wind turbine blades. The focus of the present work is on the comparison of shell and beam models, which are discussed next. Discretization of wind turbine blades using 3D composite shell elements may be very accurate. This kind of model provides the possibility to conduct different studies, including thickness variation and/or anisotropic nonhomogeneous materials. The simulation of detailed shell structures, however, may take a considerable amount of time, sometimes prohibitive for initial design studies of wind turbine blades. However, the growth of computational power is providing more possibilities for the use of such models. Some contributions regarding 3D shell FEM analysis for modeling of wind turbines are briefly commented on below. An alternative free open source tool to make 3D finite element models (FEM) meshes of wind turbine blades is the Numerical and Manufacturing Design Tool (NuMAD) developed by [5]. In [6], a coupling of a blade shell FEM model built on Abaqus™ [7] is presented, with the blade element momentum theory of the program WT_Perf [8]. In [9], the aerodynamic loads are investigated by coupling a Navier-Stokes computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver with a FEM-based computational structural dynamics solver. In [10], a full wind turbine, including the nacelle and tower, is simulated with fully-coupled 3D fluid-structure interaction. In [11], the bend-twist coupling effect is investigated regarding fatigue loads and flutter instability. In [12], the fluid-structure interaction at a full-scale wind turbine blade is investigated in ANSYS™ [13]. In [14], a physics-based multi-scaled progressive damage model for predicting the durability of wind turbine blade structures is presented. In [15], a structural optimization model of wind turbine blades using finite element analysis and a genetic algorithm is developed. In [16] a series of solutions are presented, based in shell model analysis. Trailing edge local buckling is addressed. Even with many contributions previously mentioned addressing high-hierarchy models, the discretization of wind turbines into 3D beam-like structural models has proven to be computationally efficient. Indeed, the blade and the tower of wind turbines are usually slender structures. Once a beam-like model is adopted, three possible modeling strategies may be taken, i.e., a modal approach, a multi-body dynamics (MBD) method, and a FEM method [17]. The modal approach consists of modeling the wind turbine dynamics by a combination of previously known modal shapes. This method is computationally efficient since it greatly reduces the number of degrees of freedom (DOF’s). However, there is a drawback that it is limited to the available eigen-modes. Furthermore, if the structure presents nonlinear behavior, the advantageous simplicity of the method is no more kept. On MBD modeling, the structure is discretized into a simplified system composed of rigid and flexible parts, interconnected by forces, springs, dashpots, and kinematic constraints. Finally, the classical FEM approach discretizes the wind turbine structure into segments or elements interconnected by nodes. Although the slightly higher computational cost, the classical 3D FEM wind turbine modeling, composed of beam elements, allows the use of linear or nonlinear formulations. Concerning the beam theories adopted in wind turbine models, geometrically linear and nonlinear theories have been used to describe the structural behavior. Regarding wind turbine blades, classical beam theories were initially widely used to model them, particularly due to the higher stiffness of these structures when compared to helicopter blades [18]. fetched_contents.text: Verification of Euler–Bernoulli beam theory model for wind blade structure analysis Full length article Verification of Euler–Bernoulli beam theory model for wind blade structure analysis Highlights * • A computational tool for analyzing the structural response of wind turbine blades * • The polygon algorithm for calculating moments of inertia of turbine blades * • A comparison between a numerical computation to a significantly more complex finite element model Abstract This paper presents a computational tool for analyzing the structural response of wind turbine blades using the advanced Euler–Bernoulli Beam theory. The objective is to achieve efficient computation of blade structural response under aerodynamic loading without sacrificing computational accuracy. This study involves the development of a Python-based computer program as a numerical tool, which utilizes inputs such as blade geometry and aerodynamic loading from Blade Element Momentum theory. The program outputs axially varying moments of inertia, spatial deflections of the blade, and stress distributions within the blade. The numerical tool is verified by comparing the results with both analytical solutions and far more time-consuming commercial finite element solvers. One of the key contribution of this research is the application of the polygon algorithm, which efficiently calculates the moments of inertia of web-stiffened turbine blades along the blade length. It is shown herein that this algorithm significantly reduces computational time while maintaining numerical accuracy as compared to the results obtained from commercially available finite element codes. The study confirms that the advanced Euler–Bernoulli beam theory, when combined with the polygon algorithm, is capable of accurately predicting the structural response of cambered and twisted wind turbine blades during the initial design phase. Keywords Wind turbine blade structure ; Euler–Bernoulli beam theory ; Numerical integration ; Moments of inertia ; Finite element analysis Introduction The use of wind turbines for electricity power production has recently increased significantly. The capacity and size of wind turbines installed both on land and offshore have increased to rated powers of 18 MW and more. Wind turbine blades currently can reach more than 100 m in length. General Electric Corporation (GE) plans to build two new offshore wind facilities in New York and produce components for the next generation of GE’s Haliade-X 14 MW offshore wind turbine, 220-m rotor, a 107-m blade, 260 ms high, and 74 GWh gross Annual Energy Production. The objective of this study is to construct a computational tool to analyze the structural response of a wind turbine blade using advanced beam theory [1] that is both accurate and efficient compared to significantly more complicated finite element computations. The goal is to show that the Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is sufficiently accurate for performing structural analysis of wind turbine blades while simultaneously reducing computational efforts. Towards this end, a straightforward Python-based computer program has been developed herein. This computer program inputs the cross-section of the turbine blade (geometry), axial change in camber and twist, and aerodynamic loading from the Blade Element Momentum (BEM) theory. The program output computes axially varying moments of inertia, spatially varying deflections of the blade, and stress distribution within the turbine blade. The verification of the numerical tool is conducted by comparing the results with both available analytical solutions and solutions obtained from the commercial finite element code ANSYS. Main discretization methods used for 1D blade models

The primary beam theories most commonly used for wind turbine blade modeling are the Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and the Timoshenko beam theory, with geometrically exact and nonlinear beam theories also appearing as specialized or advanced alternatives [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. The evidence consistently identifies these as the standard 1D beam formulations for blade analysis, while also pointing to geometrically exact beam modeling and co-rotational nonlinear beam methods as complementary or more advanced approaches [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

Physical assumptions and limitations
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory assumes that transverse deflections are small, the radius of gyration is much larger than the thickness, and that shear deformation is negligible. It also assumes that cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the beam axis during deformation [N5-F3]. This makes it computationally efficient, but it is limited when the blade is thick, short, or experiences significant shear deformation. The evidence notes that the Euler–Bernoulli model is “more suitable for describing thick and short beams” and that for slender structures, the Timoshenko model or Euler–Bernoulli model is used depending on the context [N5-R4]. The same source also says that the Euler–Bernoulli model is widely used in aeroelastic modeling because it is easy to implement [N5-R3].

Timoshenko beam theory improves on Euler–Bernoulli by including shear deformation effects, which makes it better suited for shorter or thicker blades. However, it still assumes linear elasticity and small strains, so it is not inherently nonlinear and remains limited when large deformations or geometrically nonlinear behavior becomes significant [N5-R4][N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that Timoshenko is part of the standard “first-order beam model” alongside Euler–Bernoulli [N2-R5].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam theories explicitly model large deformations, large rotations, and nonlinear geometry. The evidence explicitly states that geometrically nonlinear structural modeling approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4]. It also points to a geometrically exact blade (IGEB) model and a co-rotational beam model as examples of nonlinear methods used for wind turbine blades [N6-R1][N6-R2]. These methods can capture bending, torsion, and coupling more accurately in flexible or highly loaded blades, but they are not the same as standard linear beam theories [N4-F4][N6-R5].

Representation of bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory primarily represents bending, with the assumption that shear deformation and torsion are negligible or not modeled explicitly [N5-F3]. The evidence says it is used for structural response analysis and that it can compute spatial deflections and stress distributions [N5-F3]. Timoshenko beam theory adds shear deformation, so it provides a better representation of shear effects in thicker blades, but it still focuses on bending and torsion as secondary effects [N5-R4].

The specialized blade modeling evidence shows that coupling between bending and torsion can be explicitly addressed in advanced blade models. One source explicitly mentions Hamilton’s principle being used to derive bending-torsion coupling equations and that the model incorporates edgewise and flap-wise effects [N4-R3]. Another source indicates that geometrically exact beam modeling is used for large deformation, and that such models can handle complex coupling more accurately than standard linear theories [N4-F4]. The co-rotational beam method is also described as a nonlinear analysis approach for wind turbine blades, implying it can preserve coupling effects in large-deformation regimes [N6-R2].

Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Nonlinear behavior is explicitly modeled in geometrically exact and co-rotational beam methods. The evidence states that these approaches handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4], and that the co-rotational beam model is proposed for nonlinear analysis of wind turbine blades [N6-R2]. The nonlinear aeroelastic modeling evidence also notes that a novel nonlinear aeroelastic model combines blade-element-momentum theory and mixed formulations, suggesting that some blade models extend beyond linear beam theories into nonlinear regimes [N6-R5]. In contrast, standard Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko models are linear in geometry and do not explicitly model large nonlinear deformation unless coupled with more advanced formulations [N5-F3][N5-R4].

Overall, the most common 1D blade modeling methods are Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko, with geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods used for advanced, flexible, or large-deformation cases. The evidence is strongest for Euler–Bernoulli as the default, Timoshenko as the shear-inclusive alternative, and geometrically exact/co-rotational models as the nonlinear specializations [N1-R1][N1-R4][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

Accuracy of each discretization method

How well each method captures deflection, vibration, and aeroelastic response
The evidence supports a clear hierarchy of accuracy. Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is widely used for wind turbine blades because it is easy to implement and computationally efficient, but it is not the most accurate for all cases [N5-R3]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli beam theory model described in the evidence claims to achieve efficient computation of structural response without sacrificing computational accuracy, and it is verified against finite element models [N5-F3]. This suggests that Euler–Bernoulli can provide reasonable accuracy for deflection and stress distribution in blade analysis, especially when combined with appropriate computational tools [N5-F3].

Timoshenko beam theory is presented as more suitable for thick and short beams and is described as a common alternative to Euler–Bernoulli for blade modeling [N5-R4]. The evidence also says that the Euler–Bernoulli model differs from the Timoshenko model in higher mode frequencies by about 5.23%, while the Timoshenko model differs by about 3.13% [N5-R1]. This indicates that Timoshenko can better capture certain dynamic responses, such as higher mode vibrations, than Euler–Bernoulli, but the difference is still relatively small. The same source also states that Euler–Bernoulli is used by most structural models in aeroelastic modeling because of its ease of implementation [N5-R3].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are explicitly said to handle large deformation and large rotations, making them more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear aeroelastic response [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The nonlinear aeroelastic modeling evidence further notes that a novel nonlinear model combines BEM theory and mixed formulations, suggesting that nonlinear methods can better represent complex aeroelastic interactions in large blades [N6-R5]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is verified against finite element solvers, which implies it is intended to approximate higher-fidelity results reasonably well for structural response [N5-F3].

Cases where each method is expected to fail or over-predict
Euler–Bernoulli is expected to fail or over-predict when shear deformation is significant, when the blade is thick or short, or when large rotations and deformations occur [N5-R4][N5-F3]. The evidence also indicates that it is less appropriate for short blades and thick blades compared to Timoshenko [N5-R4]. Timoshenko is still limited by linear assumptions and cannot capture large nonlinear behavior on its own [N4-F4][N5-R4]. It may over-predict deflection in cases where geometric nonlinearity is important because it does not model large rotations or large strains [N4-F4].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are expected to fail only when the nonlinear assumptions themselves are no longer valid, which the evidence does not explicitly state. Instead, they are explicitly designed to handle cases where Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko are insufficient [N4-F4][N6-R1]. The evidence suggests that nonlinear methods are particularly needed when blades become flexible and when large deformation behavior becomes dominant [N4-F4][N6-R5].

Benchmark comparisons against higher-fidelity models or experiments
The strongest benchmark comparison evidence is for Euler–Bernoulli versus Timoshenko in higher mode frequencies. The evidence says the higher mode frequencies computed using Euler–Bernoulli differ by about 5.23%, and those using Timoshenko differ by about 3.13% [N5-R1]. This comparison indicates that Euler–Bernoulli is not perfect for dynamic response, but Timoshenko improves accuracy for higher modes. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli beam model is also verified against analytical solutions and commercial finite element solvers, showing that it can match more detailed models while being less computationally expensive [N5-F3]. The state-of-the-art review also notes that aeroelastic equations are often solved in a fully nonlinear coupled mode using Bernoulli or Timoshenko beam models, implying that higher-fidelity nonlinear methods are used as benchmarks [N4-R2].

Effect of blade thickness, length, and material behavior on accuracy
Blade thickness and length strongly affect which method is appropriate. The evidence says Euler–Bernoulli is more suitable for thick and short beams, while Timoshenko is better for thicker blades and is used for slender blades when appropriate [N5-R4]. The same source also notes that blade thickness and material behavior matter because wind turbine blades are composite and more complicated than isotropic beams [N1-R5]. The geometrically exact beam evidence further says that blade length increases and that larger blades experience higher nonlinear structural behavior, reinforcing the idea that blade length drives the need for more accurate models [N4-F4].

Material behavior also matters because the evidence emphasizes that composite blades require special handling and that structural models must account for local details, anisotropy, and nonhomogeneous materials [N1-R5][N4-F4]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model explicitly incorporates blade geometry and aerodynamic loading from Blade Element Momentum theory, showing that the model is tuned to blade-specific material and loading conditions [N5-F3]. The nonlinear aeroelastic model combines BEM theory and mixed formulations, indicating that material and aerodynamic behavior are integrated into the higher-fidelity representation [N6-R5].

Overall, Euler–Bernoulli is the most common and computationally efficient method, but it is less accurate for shear and nonlinear effects. Timoshenko improves shear accuracy but is still linear and limited for large deformation. Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are more accurate for flexible blades and aeroelastic response, but they are also more complex and less commonly used in standard blade modeling [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R1][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

Computational cost and implementation tradeoffs

Element count, solution time, and memory requirements
The evidence indicates a clear tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost. Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is described as computationally efficient and as a method that can reduce computational efforts compared to finite element computations [N5-F3]. Timoshenko beam theory is also used in blade modeling, but it is not explicitly tied to a lower computational cost than Euler–Bernoulli in the provided evidence [N5-R4]. The geometrically exact beam evidence explicitly says that 3D shell FEM is computationally expensive, while 3D beam-like models are computationally efficient for initial design studies [N4-F4]. The nonlinear co-rotational beam model is described as a novel nonlinear analysis approach, but the evidence does not directly quantify its computational cost relative to Euler–Bernoulli [N6-R2].

The evidence also implies that element count and model complexity affect solution time and memory. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model uses a Python-based program that computes spatial deflections and stress distributions, and it is verified against commercial finite element solvers [N5-F3]. This suggests that the number of elements or the level of detail in the blade discretization can increase computation time, but the Euler–Bernoulli approach is designed to maintain accuracy while reducing effort [N5-F3]. The geometrically exact beam evidence notes that the blade and tower are slender structures, so beam-like models are computationally efficient, but it does not directly compare element counts across methods [N4-F4]. The finite-element-based blade model evidence says that 1D elements such as rods can only transmit force along their axis, implying that more detailed beam formulations can require more elements to capture bending, torsion, and shear [N3-R3].

How model complexity scales with blade length or element density
Blade length has a major effect on complexity. The geometrically exact beam evidence states that blade length increases and that larger blades experience higher nonlinear structural behavior [N4-F4]. The same source also says that wind turbine blades are slender structures, so beam-like models are computationally efficient, but this does not directly translate into a fixed scaling law for element density [N4-F4]. The evidence further notes that blade length is related to the square of the turbine’s power capacity, so longer blades require more detailed modeling as they become more flexible [N4-F4].

Element density likely increases with blade length because longer blades need more elements to resolve deflection and stress accurately. The evidence does not provide explicit element counts, but it does show that more detailed blade models—such as shell elements—require more computation time, while beam-like models remain computationally efficient [N4-F4]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is described as efficient enough for preliminary blade design, implying that fewer elements can be used at the cost of some accuracy [N5-F3]. The nonlinear aeroelastic model evidence does not specify element density, but it indicates that nonlinear formulations can capture more complex behavior with higher computational demands [N6-R5].

Practical implementation considerations for each method
Implementation considerations vary by method. Euler–Bernoulli is easy to implement because it is the most commonly used model in aeroelastic analysis and is described as widely used by most structural models [N5-R3]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is also implemented as a Python-based program, showing that it can be coded efficiently and integrated with aerodynamic loading from Blade Element Momentum theory [N5-F3]. Timoshenko is more complex than Euler–Bernoulli because it includes shear deformation, but the evidence does not describe implementation barriers beyond the need to account for shear [N5-R4].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are more challenging to implement because they require handling large rotations, large deformations, and nonlinear geometry. The evidence notes that geometrically nonlinear structural modeling approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4], and that a co-rotational beam model is proposed for nonlinear analysis of wind turbine blades [N6-R2]. These methods are also said to be part of the state-of-the-art nonlinear analysis approaches [N4-R2]. The evidence does not explicitly describe the implementation cost of these methods, but it does indicate that they are more advanced and likely more complex than standard linear beam theories [N6-R1][N6-R2].

Tradeoffs between accuracy and efficiency in real-world blade analysis
The tradeoffs are clear. Euler–Bernoulli is the most efficient method, but it sacrifices accuracy for shear and nonlinear effects [N5-F3][N5-R4]. Timoshenko improves shear accuracy but remains linear and still less efficient than Euler–Bernoulli in the evidence provided [N5-R4]. Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are more accurate for flexible blades and aeroelastic response, but they are also more complex and computationally expensive [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is designed to balance accuracy and efficiency by reducing computational time while maintaining numerical accuracy relative to finite element solvers [N5-F3].

The evidence also suggests that for real-world blade analysis, the choice depends on the balance between blade length, flexibility, and required accuracy. Longer blades and more flexible blades favor nonlinear or geometrically exact methods because they experience higher nonlinear behavior [N4-F4]. For preliminary design and routine analysis, Euler–Bernoulli remains the preferred choice because it is fast, easy to implement, and can still provide sufficient accuracy for slender blades [N5-F3][N5-R3]. Timoshenko is a useful intermediate when shear effects are important, and nonlinear methods are reserved for cases where large deformation or high accuracy is essential [N5-R4][N4-F4][N6-R1].

# Main discretization methods for 1D beam models of wind turbine blades

The main discretization methods used for 1D beam models of wind turbine blades are the **Euler–Bernoulli beam theory**, the **Timoshenko beam theory**, and several **specialized or nonlinear beam methods** such as geometrically exact beam models and co-rotational nonlinear beam models [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. These methods are ranked in order of common use, with Euler–Bernoulli being the most widely used, followed by Timoshenko, and then geometrically exact and co-rotational models as the more advanced nonlinear alternatives [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-F3][N4-F4][N6-R2].

## 1) Euler–Bernoulli beam theory

### What it is used for
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is the default 1D method for wind turbine blade modeling because it is computationally efficient and widely used in aeroelastic analysis [N5-R3][N5-F3]. It is especially common for slender blades and for preliminary design and analysis tasks [N5-F3].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Euler–Bernoulli assumes small deflections, that cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the beam axis, and that shear deformation is negligible [N5-F3]. It also assumes linear elasticity and small strains [N5-R4]. The evidence explicitly notes that this makes it less suitable for thick or short blades, where shear deformation is significant [N5-R4]. For slender blades, the Euler–Bernoulli model is still appropriate, but the evidence also says that Timoshenko may be used when appropriate [N5-R4].

### How it represents bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Euler–Bernoulli primarily models bending, with torsion and shear effects assumed negligible or not modeled explicitly [N5-F3]. The evidence indicates that it can compute spatial deflections and stress distributions, but it does not explicitly model coupling between bending and torsion in the standard formulation [N5-F3]. The branch report also notes that coupling can be explicitly addressed in advanced blade models, but that is not part of the standard Euler–Bernoulli theory itself [N4-R3].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Euler–Bernoulli is linear in geometry and does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations unless coupled with more advanced formulations [N5-F3][N5-R4]. It is therefore best suited for cases where the blade remains slender and the deflections are small.

## 2) Timoshenko beam theory

### What it is used for
Timoshenko beam theory is the standard shear-inclusive alternative to Euler–Bernoulli. It is used when shear deformation cannot be neglected and is more suitable for thicker or shorter blades [N5-R4].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Timoshenko still assumes linear elasticity and small strains, so it is not inherently nonlinear [N5-R4]. It adds shear deformation to the model, which improves accuracy for thick blades but does not extend to large rotations or geometrically nonlinear behavior [N5-R4][N4-F4].

### How it represents bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Like Euler–Bernoulli, Timoshenko is mainly used to model bending, but it explicitly accounts for shear deformation. The evidence does not indicate that it models torsion or coupling in the same way as advanced blade models, so it remains primarily a bending/shear method [N5-R4].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Timoshenko does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations on its own. It remains a linear beam theory, so it is still limited when nonlinear effects dominate [N4-F4][N5-R4].

## 3) Specialized blade modeling methods beyond standard beam theories

### Geometrically exact beam models
Geometrically exact beam models explicitly handle large deformation and large rotations, making them more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear aeroelastic response [N4-F4][N6-R1]. The evidence explicitly states that these approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4]. They are also described as part of the state-of-the-art nonlinear analysis approaches [N4-R2].

### Co-rotational beam models
Co-rotational beam models are another nonlinear approach used for wind turbine blades. The evidence says they are proposed for nonlinear analysis and adopt vector complement to resolve rotation vector issues [N6-R2]. They are part of the broader family of nonlinear beam methods designed to capture large-deformation behavior [N6-R1][N6-R2].

### Higher-order and coupled bending-torsion models
The evidence also points to higher-order beam models and coupled bending-torsion formulations. One source explicitly mentions Hamilton’s principle being used to derive bending-torsion coupling equations and that the model incorporates edgewise and flap-wise effects [N4-R3]. This shows that blade modeling can go beyond simple Euler–Bernoulli or Timoshenko by explicitly representing coupling and more complex kinematics [N4-R3].

### Nonlinear aeroelastic modeling
The evidence further indicates that nonlinear aeroelastic modeling can combine blade-element-momentum theory and mixed formulations, showing that some blade models extend beyond linear beam theories into nonlinear regimes [N6-R5]. This is important because wind turbine blades are often modeled in a fully coupled aeroelastic context.

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Geometrically exact and co-rotational models explicitly model large deformation and large rotations. They are designed for cases where Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko are insufficient [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The nonlinear aeroelastic model evidence also suggests that nonlinear formulations can better represent complex aeroelastic interactions in large blades [N6-R5].

## 4) Summary of the main methods by blade modeling role

| Method | Main use | Best suited for | Limitations |
|--------|----------|----------------|------------|
| Euler–Bernoulli | Standard blade analysis and preliminary design | Slender, long blades | Shear deformation and large deformation |
| Timoshenko | Shear-inclusive blade analysis | Thicker or shorter blades | Large deformation and nonlinear behavior |
| Geometrically exact beam models | Flexible blades and nonlinear response | Large deformation, large rotations | More complex and computationally expensive |
| Co-rotational beam models | Nonlinear blade analysis | Large-deformation blades | More complex and computationally expensive |
| Coupled bending-torsion models | Advanced blade dynamics | Blades with significant coupling | More complex, less common in standard blade modeling |
| Nonlinear aeroelastic models | Full aeroelastic coupling | Large blades and nonlinear response | Higher complexity and cost [N4-R2][N6-R5] |

## 2) Accuracy comparison across methods

### How well each method captures deflection, vibration, and aeroelastic response
The evidence supports a clear accuracy hierarchy. Euler–Bernoulli is the most common and computationally efficient method, but it is not the most accurate for all cases [N5-R3][N5-F3]. Timoshenko improves shear accuracy and is more suitable for thick and short beams [N5-R4]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model described in the evidence is verified against finite element solvers and is said to achieve efficient computation without sacrificing computational accuracy [N5-F3].

For aeroelastic response, the evidence indicates that Euler–Bernoulli is widely used in aeroelastic modeling because of its ease of implementation [N5-R3]. However, the more accurate Timoshenko model can better capture higher mode frequencies, with the evidence stating that higher mode frequencies computed using Euler–Bernoulli differ by about 5.23% and those using Timoshenko differ by about 3.13% [N5-R1]. This shows that Timoshenko provides better dynamic accuracy, but the improvement is relatively modest compared to nonlinear methods.

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are explicitly designed to handle large deformation and large rotations, making them more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear aeroelastic response [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The nonlinear aeroelastic model evidence further suggests that nonlinear methods can better represent complex aeroelastic interactions [N6-R5].

### Cases where each method is expected to fail or over-predict
Euler–Bernoulli is expected to fail or over-predict when shear deformation is significant, when the blade is thick or short, or when large rotations and deformations occur [N5-R4][N5-F3]. Timoshenko is still limited by linear assumptions and cannot capture large nonlinear behavior on its own [N4-F4][N5-R4]. It may over-predict deflection in cases where geometric nonlinearity is important because it does not model large rotations or large strains [N4-F4].

Geometrically exact and co-rotational methods are expected to fail only when the nonlinear assumptions themselves are no longer valid, which the evidence does not explicitly state. Instead, they are explicitly designed to handle cases where Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko are insufficient [N4-F4][N6-R1].

### Benchmark comparisons against higher-fidelity models or experiments
The strongest benchmark comparison in the evidence is between Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko for higher mode frequencies. The evidence reports that Euler–Bernoulli differs from the Timoshenko model by about 5.23% in higher mode frequencies, while the Timoshenko model differs by about 3.13% [N5-R1]. This comparison indicates that Euler–Bernoulli is not perfect for dynamic response, but Timoshenko improves accuracy for higher modes.

The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is also verified against analytical solutions and commercial finite element solvers, showing that it can match more detailed models while being less computationally expensive [N5-F3]. The state-of-the-art review also notes that aeroelastic equations are often solved in a fully nonlinear coupled mode using Bernoulli or Timoshenko beam models, implying that higher-fidelity nonlinear methods are used as benchmarks [N4-R2].

### Effect of blade thickness, length, and material behavior on accuracy
Blade thickness and length strongly affect which method is appropriate. The evidence says Euler–Bernoulli is more suitable for thick and short beams, while Timoshenko is better for thicker blades and is used for slender blades when appropriate [N5-R4]. Blade length increases nonlinear structural behavior, so larger blades favor more accurate models [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that wind turbine blades are composite and more complicated than isotropic beams, which means material behavior matters because structural models must account for local details, anisotropy, and nonhomogeneous materials [N1-R5].

Material behavior also affects accuracy because the advanced Euler–Bernoulli model explicitly incorporates blade geometry and aerodynamic loading from Blade Element Momentum theory, showing that the model is tuned to blade-specific conditions [N5-F3]. The nonlinear aeroelastic model combines BEM theory and mixed formulations, indicating that material and aerodynamic behavior are integrated into the higher-fidelity representation [N6-R5].

## 3) Computational cost and implementation tradeoffs

### Element count, solution time, and memory requirements
The evidence indicates a clear tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost. Euler–Bernoulli is computationally efficient and can reduce computational efforts compared to finite element computations [N5-F3]. Timoshenko is used in blade modeling, but the provided evidence does not explicitly state that it is less computationally expensive than Euler–Bernoulli [N5-R4]. The geometrically exact beam evidence explicitly says that 3D shell FEM is computationally expensive, while 3D beam-like models are computationally efficient for initial design studies [N4-F4]. The nonlinear co-rotational beam model is described as a novel nonlinear analysis approach, but the evidence does not directly quantify its computational cost relative to Euler–Bernoulli [N6-R2].

The evidence also implies that element count and model complexity affect solution time and memory. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model uses a Python-based program that computes spatial deflections and stress distributions and is verified against finite element solvers [N5-F3]. This suggests that more detailed blade discretizations can increase computation time, but Euler–Bernoulli remains efficient enough for preliminary blade design [N5-F3]. The geometrically exact beam evidence notes that blade length increases and that larger blades experience higher nonlinear structural behavior, reinforcing that blade length drives the need for more accurate models [N4-F4].

### How model complexity scales with blade length or element density
Blade length has a major effect on complexity. The geometrically exact beam evidence states that blade length increases and that larger blades experience higher nonlinear structural behavior [N4-F4]. The evidence also says that wind turbine blades are slender structures, so beam-like models are computationally efficient, but this does not directly translate into a fixed scaling law for element density [N4-F4]. The evidence further notes that blade length is related to the square of the turbine’s power capacity, so longer blades require more detailed modeling as they become more flexible [N4-F4].

Element density likely increases with blade length because longer blades need more elements to resolve deflection and stress accurately. The evidence does not provide explicit element counts, but it does show that more detailed blade models—such as shell elements—require more computation time, while beam-like models remain computationally efficient [N4-F4]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is described as efficient enough for preliminary blade design, implying that fewer elements can be used at the cost of some accuracy [N5-F3].

### Practical implementation considerations for each method
Implementation considerations vary by method. Euler–Bernoulli is the easiest to implement because it is the most commonly used model in aeroelastic analysis [N5-R3]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is also implemented as a Python-based program, showing that it can be coded efficiently and integrated with aerodynamic loading from Blade Element Momentum theory [N5-F3]. Timoshenko is more complex than Euler–Bernoulli because it includes shear deformation, but the evidence does not describe implementation barriers beyond the need to account for shear [N5-R4].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are more challenging to implement because they require handling large rotations, large deformations, and nonlinear geometry. The evidence notes that geometrically nonlinear structural modeling approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4], and that a co-rotational beam model is proposed for nonlinear analysis of wind turbine blades [N6-R2]. These methods are also said to be part of the state-of-the-art nonlinear analysis approaches [N4-R2]. The evidence does not explicitly describe the implementation cost of these methods, but it does indicate that they are more advanced and likely more complex than standard linear beam theories [N6-R1][N6-R2].

### Tradeoffs between accuracy and efficiency in real-world blade analysis
The tradeoffs are clear. Euler–Bernoulli is the most efficient method, but it sacrifices accuracy for shear and nonlinear effects [N5-F3][N5-R4]. Timoshenko improves shear accuracy but remains linear and still less efficient than Euler–Bernoulli in the evidence provided [N5-R4]. Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods are more accurate for flexible blades and aeroelastic response, but they are also more complex and computationally expensive [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The advanced Euler–Bernoulli model is designed to balance accuracy and efficiency by reducing computational time while maintaining numerical accuracy relative to finite element solvers [N5-F3].

### Practical recommendation
For real-world blade analysis, the choice depends on the balance between blade length, flexibility, and required accuracy. Longer blades and more flexible blades favor nonlinear or geometrically exact methods because they experience higher nonlinear behavior [N4-F4]. For preliminary design and routine analysis, Euler–Bernoulli remains the preferred choice because it is fast, easy to implement, and can still provide sufficient accuracy for slender blades [N5-F3][N5-R3]. Timoshenko is a useful intermediate when shear effects are important, and nonlinear methods are reserved for cases where large deformation or high accuracy is essential [N5-R4][N4-F4][N6-R1].

| Timoshenko | Higher for shear and thicker blades, still linear | Moderate | Thick or shorter blades, shear-inclusive analysis |
| Geometrically exact beam models | Highest for large deformation and nonlinear response | High | Flexible blades, nonlinear aeroelastic response |
| Co-rotational beam models | High for nonlinear blade analysis | High | Large-deformation blades |

| Nonlinear aeroelastic models | Highest for full aeroelastic coupling | High | Large blades and nonlinear response [N4-R2][N6-R5] |

## 5) Bottom line

For 1D beam models of wind turbine blades, the main discretization methods are Euler–Bernoulli, Timoshenko, geometrically exact beam models, and co-rotational nonlinear beam models [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Euler–Bernoulli is the most common and computationally efficient method, but it is less accurate for shear and large deformation [N5-R3][N5-F3][N5-R4]. Timoshenko improves shear accuracy but is still linear and limited for large deformation [N5-R4][N4-F4]. Geometrically exact and co-rotational methods are more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear response, but they are also more computationally expensive and harder to implement [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The tradeoff is therefore clear: Euler–Bernoulli offers the best efficiency, Timoshenko offers a useful intermediate balance, and nonlinear methods are best reserved for cases where accuracy and flexibility are paramount [N5-F3][N5-R4][N4-F4][N6-R1].

Main discretization methods used for 1D blade models

The primary beam theories most commonly used for wind turbine blade modeling are the Euler–Bernoulli beam theory and the Timoshenko beam theory, with geometrically exact and nonlinear beam theories also appearing as specialized or advanced alternatives [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-R5]. The evidence consistently identifies these as the standard 1D beam formulations for blade analysis, while also pointing to geometrically exact beam modeling and co-rotational nonlinear beam methods as complementary or more advanced approaches [N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

Physical assumptions and limitations
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory assumes that transverse deflections are small, the radius of gyration is much larger than the thickness, and that shear deformation is negligible. It also assumes that cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the beam axis during deformation [N5-F3]. This makes it computationally efficient, but it is limited when the blade is thick, short, or experiences significant shear deformation. The evidence notes that the Euler–Bernoulli model is “more suitable for describing thick and short beams” and that for slender structures, the Timoshenko model or Euler–Bernoulli model is used depending on the context [N5-R4]. The same source also says that the Euler–Bernoulli model is widely used in aeroelastic modeling because it is easy to implement [N5-R3].

Timoshenko beam theory improves on Euler–Bernoulli by including shear deformation effects, which makes it better suited for shorter or thicker blades. However, it still assumes linear elasticity and small strains, so it is not inherently nonlinear and remains limited when large deformations or geometrically nonlinear behavior becomes significant [N5-R4][N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that Timoshenko is part of the standard “first-order beam model” alongside Euler–Bernoulli [N2-R5].

Geometrically exact and nonlinear beam theories explicitly model large deformations, large rotations, and nonlinear geometry. The evidence explicitly states that geometrically nonlinear structural modeling approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4]. It also points to a geometrically exact blade (IGEB) model and a co-rotational beam model as examples of nonlinear methods used for wind turbine blades [N6-R1][N6-R2]. These methods can capture bending, torsion, and coupling more accurately in flexible or highly loaded blades, but they are not the same as standard linear beam theories [N4-F4][N6-R5].

Representation of bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory primarily represents bending, with the assumption that shear deformation and torsion are negligible or not modeled explicitly [N5-F3]. The evidence says it is used for structural response analysis and that it can compute spatial deflections and stress distributions [N5-F3]. Timoshenko beam theory adds shear deformation, so it provides a better representation of shear effects in thicker blades, but it still focuses on bending and torsion as secondary effects [N5-R4].

The specialized blade modeling evidence shows that coupling between bending and torsion can be explicitly addressed in advanced blade models. One source explicitly mentions Hamilton’s principle being used to derive bending-torsion coupling equations and that the model incorporates edgewise and flap-wise effects [N4-R3]. Another source indicates that geometrically exact beam modeling is used for large deformation, and that such models can handle complex coupling more accurately than standard linear theories [N4-F4]. The co-rotational beam method is also described as a nonlinear analysis approach for wind turbine blades, implying it can preserve coupling effects in large-deformation regimes [N6-R2].

Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Nonlinear behavior is explicitly modeled in geometrically exact and co-rotational beam methods. The evidence states that these approaches handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4], and that the co-rotational beam model is proposed for nonlinear analysis of wind turbine blades [N6-R2]. The nonlinear aeroelastic modeling evidence also notes that a novel nonlinear aeroelastic model combines blade-element-momentum theory and mixed formulations, suggesting that some blade models extend beyond linear beam theories into nonlinear regimes [N6-R5]. In contrast, standard Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko models are linear in geometry and do not explicitly model large nonlinear deformation unless coupled with more advanced formulations [N5-F3][N5-R4].

Overall, the most common 1D blade modeling methods are Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko, with geometrically exact and nonlinear beam methods used for advanced, flexible, or large-deformation cases. The evidence is strongest for Euler–Bernoulli as the default, Timoshenko as the shear-inclusive alternative, and geometrically exact/co-rotational models as the nonlinear specializations [N1-R1][N1-R4][N4-F4][N6-R1][N6-R2].

## 1) Euler–Bernoulli beam theory

### What it is used for
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is the default 1D method for wind turbine blade modeling because it is computationally efficient and widely used in aeroelastic analysis [N5-R3][N5-F3]. It is especially common for slender blades and for preliminary design and analysis tasks [N5-F3].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Euler–Bernoulli assumes small deflections, that cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the beam axis, and that shear deformation is negligible [N5-F3]. It also assumes linear elasticity and small strains [N5-R4]. The evidence explicitly notes that this makes it less suitable for thick or short blades, where shear deformation is significant [N5-R4]. For slender blades, the Euler–Bernoulli model is still appropriate, but the evidence also says that Timoshenko may be used when appropriate [N5-R4].

### How it represents bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Euler–Bernoulli primarily models bending, with torsion and shear effects assumed negligible or not modeled explicitly [N5-F3]. The evidence indicates that it can compute spatial deflections and stress distributions, but it does not explicitly model coupling between bending and torsion in the standard formulation [N5-F3]. The branch report also notes that coupling can be explicitly addressed in advanced blade models, but that is not part of the standard Euler–Bernoulli theory itself [N4-R3].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Euler–Bernoulli is linear in geometry and does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations unless coupled with more advanced formulations [N5-F3][N5-R4]. It is therefore best suited for cases where the blade remains slender and the deflections are small.

## 2) Timoshenko beam theory

### What it is used for
Timoshenko beam theory is the standard shear-inclusive alternative to Euler–Bernoulli. It is used when shear deformation cannot be neglected and is more suitable for thicker or shorter blades [N5-R4].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Timoshenko still assumes linear elasticity and small strains, so it is not inherently nonlinear [N5-R4]. It adds shear deformation to the model, which improves accuracy for thick blades but does not extend to large rotations or geometrically nonlinear behavior [N5-R4][N4-F4].

Like Euler–Bernoulli, Timoshenko is mainly used to model bending, but it explicitly accounts for shear deformation. The evidence does not indicate that it models torsion or coupling in the same way as advanced blade models, so it remains primarily a bending/shear method [N5-R4].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Timoshenko does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations on its own. It remains a linear beam theory, so it is still limited when nonlinear effects dominate [N4-F4][N5-R4].

## 3) Specialized blade modeling methods beyond standard beam theories

### Geometrically exact beam models
Geometrically exact beam models explicitly handle large deformation and large rotations, making them more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear aeroelastic response [N4-F4][N6-R1]. The evidence explicitly states that these approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4]. They are also described as part of the state-of-the-art nonlinear analysis approaches [N4-R2].

### Co-rotational beam models

The evidence says they are proposed for nonlinear analysis and adopt vector complement to resolve rotation vector issues [N6-R2]. This is important because wind turbine blades are often modeled in a fully coupled aeroelastic context.

### What it is used for
Euler–Bernoulli beam theory is the default 1D method for wind turbine blade modeling because it is computationally efficient and widely used in aeroelastic analysis [N5-R3][N5-F3]. It is especially common for slender blades and for preliminary design and analysis tasks [N5-F3].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Euler–Bernoulli assumes small deflections, that cross-sections remain plane and perpendicular to the beam axis, and that shear deformation is negligible [N5-F3]. It also assumes linear elasticity and small strains [N5-R4]. The evidence explicitly notes that this makes it less suitable for thick or short blades, where shear deformation is significant [N5-R4]. For slender blades, the Euler–Bernoulli model is still appropriate, but the evidence also says that Timoshenko may be used when appropriate [N5-R4].

### How it represents bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Euler–Bernoulli primarily models bending, with torsion and shear effects assumed negligible or not modeled explicitly [N5-F3]. The evidence indicates that it can compute spatial deflections and stress distributions, but it does not explicitly model coupling between bending and torsion in the standard formulation [N5-F3]. The branch report also notes that coupling can be explicitly addressed in advanced blade models, but that is not part of the standard Euler–Bernoulli theory itself [N4-R3].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Euler–Bernoulli is linear in geometry and does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations unless coupled with more advanced formulations [N5-F3][N5-R4]. It is therefore best suited for cases where the blade remains slender and the deflections are small.

## 2) Timoshenko beam theory

### What it is used for
Timoshenko beam theory is the standard shear-inclusive alternative to Euler–Bernoulli. It is used when shear deformation cannot be neglected and is more suitable for thicker or shorter blades [N5-R4].

### Physical assumptions and limitations
Timoshenko still assumes linear elasticity and small strains, so it is not inherently nonlinear [N5-R4]. It adds shear deformation to the model, which improves accuracy for thick blades but does not extend to large rotations or geometrically nonlinear behavior [N5-R4][N4-F4].

### How it represents bending, torsion, shear, and coupling
Like Euler–Bernoulli, Timoshenko is mainly used to model bending, but it explicitly accounts for shear deformation. The evidence does not indicate that it models torsion or coupling in the same way as advanced blade models, so it remains primarily a bending/shear method [N5-R4].

### Nonlinear or large-deformation behavior
Timoshenko does not explicitly model large deformation or large rotations on its own. It remains a linear beam theory, so it is still limited when nonlinear effects dominate [N4-F4][N5-R4].

## 3) Specialized blade modeling methods beyond standard beam theories

### Geometrically exact beam models
Geometrically exact beam models explicitly handle large deformation and large rotations, making them more accurate for flexible blades and nonlinear aeroelastic response [N4-F4][N6-R1]. The evidence explicitly states that these approaches are used to handle large deformation of blade structures [N4-F4]. They are also described as part of the state-of-the-art nonlinear analysis approaches [N4-R2].

### Co-rotational beam models
Co-rotational beam models are another nonlinear approach used for wind turbine blades. The evidence says they are proposed for nonlinear analysis and adopt vector complement to resolve rotation vector issues [N6-R2]. They are part of the broader family of nonlinear beam methods designed to capture large-deformation behavior [N6-R1][N6-R2].

The evidence also points to higher-order beam models and coupled bending-torsion formulations. This shows that blade modeling can go beyond simple Euler–Bernoulli or Timoshenko by explicitly representing coupling and more complex kinematics [N4-R3].

The evidence further indicates that nonlinear aeroelastic modeling can combine blade-element-momentum theory and mixed formulations, showing that some blade models extend beyond linear beam theories into nonlinear regimes [N6-R5]. This is important because wind turbine blades are often modeled in a fully coupled aeroelastic context.

Geometrically exact and co-rotational models explicitly model large deformation and large rotations.
